title: 暴风雨过后的海滩
title_en: What the Storm Leaves Behind: A Morning Hunting Fossils
summary_zh: 为了让宅在家的儿子出门，“我”报名参加了冬日海边的化石徒步。一位退休海洋生物学家让母子俩学会看见“眼皮底下”的奇迹。读完你能学会描述态度转变和细致观察的表达。
body: I signed up for the fossil walk mainly to get my teenage son out of the house, and I'll admit I was skeptical that a gray January beach could hold anyone's attention for three hours. Our guide, a retired marine biologist named Ruth, seemed to have anticipated this. Before we had even reached the waterline, she crouched down, turned over a flat stone and showed us the faint ribbed outline of a shell that, she said, had been lying there since long before there were any humans to find it. My son, who had spent the drive pretending to be asleep, leaned in for a closer look. What struck me over the next few hours was that the real skill lay not in knowing what to look for but in knowing where. Ruth talked about the geography of the coast as if it were a library whose shelves were constantly being rearranged: winter storms tear chunks out of the soft cliffs, the tide sorts whatever falls, and the probability of finding something worthwhile is highest in the brief window after a big storm and before the next high tide. She was equally firm that we keep well away from the base of the cliffs, which can collapse without warning. Not everything we found was ancient. A gull had left a crab shell on a rock, and offshore a small boat from the local fishery was working its way along a line of buoys, two figures aboard hauling up pots. At noon Ruth passed around cups of something sweet and warming from a flask, and my son, without being asked, showed her the spiral-shaped fragment he had been guarding in his palm all morning. I can't promise the day will turn him into a scientist. But I came home oddly hopeful, and it occurred to me that the things which stun us most are often not rare at all; they have simply been lying in plain sight, waiting for someone to bend down.

questions.prompt: What does the writer suggest at the end of the article?
options: Fossils are much rarer than most people believe
Remarkable things are often all around us if we look closely
Her son has decided to become a scientist
Fossil hunting is more rewarding without a guide
questions.evidence: the things which stun us most are often not rare at all; they have simply been lying in plain sight, waiting for someone to bend down

questions.prompt: According to Ruth, what gives you the best chance of finding fossils?
options: Visiting on calm summer days when the beach is quiet
Going out after a big storm, before the next high tide
Searching early in the morning, before the fishing boats go out
Looking at the base of the cliffs, where rocks have just fallen
questions.evidence: the probability of finding something worthwhile is highest in the brief window after a big storm and before the next high tide

questions.prompt: What does the son's behaviour at noon suggest?
options: He wanted to go home early
He had found something the guide had lost
He had become genuinely interested in the walk
He was hungry and bored
questions.evidence: without being asked, showed her the spiral-shaped fragment he had been guarding in his palm all morning

questions.prompt: What does "skeptical" mean in "I was skeptical that a gray January beach could hold anyone's attention"?
options: certain
doubtful
excited
frightened
questions.evidence: I was skeptical that a gray January beach could hold anyone's attention for three hours

vocabulary.example: I was skeptical about the new diet until I saw how well my sister slept.
The teacher had anticipated our questions and prepared extra examples.
She crouched next to the puppy and held out her hand.
We found a fragment of blue pottery in the garden.
They spent the morning hauling boxes up to the fourth floor.

expressions.meaning: 吸引得住任何人的注意力
expressions.note: hold sb's attention 指“持续吸引注意”，常用于否定或怀疑：The film couldn't hold my attention.

expressions.text: leaned in for a closer look
expressions.note: lean in 身体前倾，是描写好奇心被勾起的经典动作。
常和 collapse、change、happen 等词搭配，书面口语都常用。
work one's way along / through 表示逐步、费力地前进。
比 I suddenly thought 更地道，常用来引出文章结尾的感悟。

expressions.meaning: 就在眼皮底下；在最显眼的地方
expressions.note: 常见搭配 hidden in plain sight“明明就在眼前却没人发现”。

knowledge.quote: What struck me over the next few hours was that the real skill lay not in knowing what to look for but in knowing where.
knowledge.explanation: What struck me 是主语从句，that the real skill lay... 是表语从句，把“让我印象深的点”放到句末强调；not in A but in B 是 C1 常用的对照结构。

knowledge.quote: Ruth talked about the geography of the coast as if it were a library whose shelves were constantly being rearranged
knowledge.explanation: as if + were 表示与事实相反的比喻：海岸并不真是图书馆。whose 引出“书架不断被重新摆放”，被动进行时 were being rearranged 突出变化一直在发生。

knowledge.quote: they have simply been lying in plain sight, waiting for someone to bend down
knowledge.explanation: waiting 是现在分词作伴随状语，把化石拟人化：它们一直躺在那里“等”人弯腰。分词放在句末，让结尾更有余味。

speaking: 用 1 分钟描述一次你本来不感兴趣、最后却很享受的活动，说说是什么改变了你的看法，用上 I was skeptical that ... 和 it occurred to me that。
writing: 用 180–220 词写一篇短文，描写一个你常去、却最近才真正“看见”的地方（公园、街道、菜市场），结尾用 in plain sight 点题。

task.prompt: 仿照这句，用 I'll admit I was skeptical that ... could ... 写一件你起初不相信、后来改观的事。
task.model: I'll admit I was skeptical that a gray January beach could hold anyone's attention for three hours

title: 真正的善良不必“随机”
title_en: Good, Not Just Nice: The Case for Predictable Kindness
summary_zh: 社区通讯呼吁大家“每周做一件随机善事”，作者却不以为然。这篇观点文认为，真正的善良是日复一日、没人鼓掌的小事。读完你能学会委婉提出异议、层层论证的表达。
body: A while ago our neighborhood newsletter ran an editorial urging readers to commit one random act of kindness every week, and I was surprised by how much it irritated me. I have nothing against kindness, obviously; what bothered me was the word 'random' itself. Philosophers have argued for centuries about whether goodness lives in individual acts or in settled character, and while I am in no position to resolve that debate, ordinary life seems to have taken a side. The people I would nominate as genuinely good are rarely the ones who make dramatic gestures. They are the ones whose kindness is predictable. My upstairs neighbor is a fine illustration. As far as I know, she has never paid for a stranger's coffee or left an anonymous note under a windshield wiper. But for as long as I have lived here, she has taken in everyone's parcels, remembered who is allergic to what, and noticed, before anyone else, when the elderly man on the ground floor stopped collecting his mail. That kind of consistency is less photogenic than a grand gesture, and it is easy to neglect precisely because it never makes a good story. I am skeptical, too, of efforts to make kindness mandatory, as though it could be scheduled like a dental appointment or announced in an office memo. Kindness performed to meet a quota tends to look for an audience; kindness that has become habit hardly notices itself. None of this means the newsletter was wrong to try. But I would rather we stopped treating goodness as a pleasant surprise and started treating it as a practice, built slowly through small attentions that nobody applauds. That may sound less exciting. I find it far more hopeful, because it means goodness is not reserved for heroes; it is available to anyone willing to keep showing up.

questions.prompt: What is the writer's main argument?
options: Random acts of kindness do more harm than good
Real goodness shows itself in steady everyday habits rather than occasional gestures
Kindness should be organized by community groups so that it is fair
Only people born with a strong character are capable of real kindness
questions.evidence: They are the ones whose kindness is predictable.

questions.prompt: Why does the writer mention the upstairs neighbor?
options: To show that dramatic gestures are more memorable than daily habits
To give an example of quiet, reliable kindness
To complain that nobody else in the building helps the elderly man
To explain why the newsletter's idea became so popular
questions.evidence: My upstairs neighbor is a fine illustration.

questions.prompt: What does "photogenic" mean in "That kind of consistency is less photogenic"?
options: old-fashioned
attractive or impressive in pictures
easy to remember
expensive
questions.evidence: That kind of consistency is less photogenic than a grand gesture

questions.prompt: What irritated the writer about the newsletter's editorial?
options: Its call for kindness itself
The word "random"
Its mention of philosophers
Its unusual length
questions.evidence: what bothered me was the word 'random' itself

vocabulary.example: I was irritated by the constant noise from the building site.
Someone left an anonymous thank-you card on my desk.

vocabulary.meaning: 上镜的；适合拍照展示的
vocabulary.example: The little harbor town is so photogenic that everyone stops to take pictures.
He set himself a quota of ten pages of reading a day.
Nobody applauds you for washing the dishes, but someone has to do it.

expressions.note: 先表明不反对，再用 but / what bothers me 提出保留意见，是委婉表达异议的常用开头。
be in no position to do sth，谦虚地说自己没法下定论，也可用于“处境不允许”。
take a side / take sides 指在争论中支持某一方：I'm not taking sides.
给自己的说法留余地，暗示“可能有我不知道的情况”。

expressions.meaning: 坚持不懈地出现、做下去
expressions.note: show up 本义“到场”，keep showing up 引申为日复一日地坚持，鼓励类文章常用。

knowledge.quote: But I would rather we stopped treating goodness as a pleasant surprise and started treating it as a practice
knowledge.explanation: would rather + 主语 + 过去式，表达对现在或将来的愿望（“我宁愿我们……”）；stopped、started 并非指过去，而是虚拟语气。

knowledge.quote: Philosophers have argued for centuries about whether goodness lives in individual acts or in settled character
knowledge.explanation: whether ... or ... 引导名词性从句，作介词 about 的宾语，表示“是……还是……”；介词后面只能用 whether，不能用 if。

knowledge.quote: They are the ones whose kindness is predictable.
knowledge.explanation: whose 表示所属，“他们的善意是可以预料的”；whose 后面紧跟名词，既可指人也可指物。

speaking: 用 1 分钟说说你身边一个“靠谱的好人”，他／她坚持做了哪些不起眼的小事，用上 a fine illustration 和 as far as I know。
writing: 用 180–220 词写一篇观点短文：善良更多体现在偶然的善举还是日常的习惯？先用 I have nothing against ... 承认另一方，再给出你的看法，并用一个 would rather 句。

task.prompt: 仿照这句，用 I have nothing against ..., obviously; what bothered me was ... 礼貌地表达你对某件流行事物的保留意见。
task.model: I have nothing against kindness, obviously; what bothered me was the word 'random' itself.

title: 村礼堂里那架没人弹的钢琴
title_en: The Piano Nobody Played: A Village Hall Restoration
summary_zh: 村礼堂里的旧钢琴一直被当成置物架，直到一位退休作曲家决定修好它。一个社区合力修复旧物的温暖故事，读完你能学会生动叙事、描写人物态度的表达。
body: For as long as anyone could remember, the upright piano in the village hall had been used mainly as a shelf. Raffle prizes were stacked on it at the summer fair, and children occasionally banged out a few notes before being told to stop. So when Edwin, a retired composer who had recently moved into the cottage by the bridge, asked the hall committee whether he might take a look at it, most of them assumed he was simply being polite. He was not. He spent an entire afternoon inspecting it, lifting the lid, testing every key and peering at the hammers with a torch, before delivering his verdict: decades of neglect, but nothing a patient restoration couldn't put right. What followed was the most intensive piece of village cooperation anyone could recall. A retired joiner repaired the cracked casing; two teenagers, bribed with pizza, sanded the legs; Edwin himself replaced felts and strings over a long, cold winter, working in the unheated hall in fingerless gloves. The hall was not much to look at, a plain brick box said to stand on medieval foundations, but by spring the piano gleamed in one corner like something borrowed from a far grander room. The committee had printed thirty programmes for the opening evening, so the crowd that squeezed through the doors was enough to stun them. Edwin made no attempt to entertain anyone with brilliant tricks. He played a slow, simple piece he had written for the occasion, and as the final chord faded, there was a surge of applause so sudden that a toddler near the front burst into tears. Someone later suggested nominating the project for a heritage award, but Edwin waved the idea away. The point, he said, was not that the piano looked stunning again, but that it would now be played badly by children for another fifty years, which was exactly what pianos were for.

questions.prompt: What does Edwin's final comment suggest about his attitude to the piano?
options: It should be protected and played only by skilled musicians
Its value lies in being used by ordinary people rather than in how it looks
He is worried that children will undo his careful repairs
The village should now organise regular concerts with professional pianists
questions.evidence: it would now be played badly by children for another fifty years, which was exactly what pianos were for

questions.prompt: Why was the committee stunned on the opening evening?
options: Edwin played a piece that nobody had heard before
Far more people turned up than they had expected
A small child burst into tears during the performance
The piano sounded better than it ever had
questions.evidence: The committee had printed thirty programmes for the opening evening, so the crowd that squeezed through the doors was enough to stun them.

questions.prompt: What is the story mainly about?
options: A composer's career in a big city
A competition for a heritage award
A village working together to restore a neglected piano
A child learning to play the piano
questions.evidence: What followed was the most intensive piece of village cooperation anyone could recall.

questions.prompt: What does "neglect" mean in "decades of neglect"?
options: bad weather
a lack of care and attention
careful repair
heavy daily use

vocabulary.example: After tasting the soup, my grandmother gave her verdict: more salt.
We bribed the kids with ice cream to tidy their room.
The kitchen floor gleamed after he mopped it.
The toddler refused to put his shoes on.

expressions.text: For as long as anyone could remember
expressions.meaning: 自打人们记事起；一直以来
expressions.note: 故事开头的常用说法，强调某种状况由来已久。
bang out 指用力、随意地弹出或敲出，带一点吵闹感。
put sth right 是英式常用说法，修理东西或纠正错误都可以：We need to put this mistake right.
形容人或地方外表普通，常接 but 引出它的长处。
burst into + 名词表示情绪突然爆发：burst into laughter。

expressions.meaning: 摆摆手拒绝了这个主意
expressions.note: wave sth away 用手势表示不在乎、不接受，描写人物态度很生动。

knowledge.quote: For as long as anyone could remember, the upright piano in the village hall had been used mainly as a shelf.
knowledge.explanation: 过去完成时的被动语态 had been used，交代故事开始之前钢琴一直被当架子用；配合 for as long as 说明“长期如此”的背景。

knowledge.quote: children occasionally banged out a few notes before being told to stop
knowledge.explanation: 介词 before 后接动名词；孩子是“被叫停”的，所以用被动式 being told。“介词 + being done”是高级写作里的常见结构。

knowledge.quote: two teenagers, bribed with pizza, sanded the legs
knowledge.explanation: bribed 是过去分词，表示被动“被披萨收买的”，用逗号隔开插在主谓之间，补充信息又不打断主句。

speaking: 用 1 分钟讲一件被大家忽视、后来又被重新利用起来的东西（旧物、空间、技能），用上 for as long as anyone could remember 和 not much to look at。
writing: 用 180–220 词写一个小故事：一群人合力修好或完成一件事，写出过程和结局，至少用一个过去完成时和一个“介词 + being done”结构。

task.prompt: 仿照这句，用 The point, he/she said, was not that ..., but that ... 写一句话，点出一件事真正的意义。
task.model: The point, he said, was not that the piano looked stunning again, but that it would now be played badly by children for another fifty years

title: 退休老爸迷上了哲学
title_en: Dad Has Discovered Philosophy, and Sunday Lunch Will Never Be the Same
summary_zh: 教了三十多年地理的父亲退休后上了一门思想史课，开始在饭桌上追问“善良是天生的吗”。一封写给老友的家常邮件，幽默又温情，读完你能学会写信叙事、描述家人变化的表达。
body: Hi Sam, I've been meaning to write for weeks, but family life has taken a slightly bizarre turn and I needed time to process it. You'll remember that Dad retired in the spring after more than thirty years of teaching geography. We all assumed he'd take up golf or finally clear out the garage. Instead, he signed up for an intensive summer course on the history of ideas at the local college, and he has come back a changed man. He now quotes ancient philosophers over breakfast the way other people read out the weather forecast. Last Sunday, just as Mum was carving the roast, he asked whether goodness was something you were born with or something you practised, and refused to pass the potatoes until each of us had given an answer. Mum, who has a wonderfully dry sense of humour, responded by sending the whole family a memo, printed and stuck to the fridge, declaring that philosophical questions are banned before ten in the morning and that attendance at Sunday lunch remains mandatory, whatever anyone's views on free will. Honestly, though, I've started to enjoy it. On the ferry over to see them last weekend, he spent the entire crossing explaining a medieval puzzle about a donkey that starves because it can't choose between two identical piles of hay, and by the time we docked, half the passengers aboard had joined the argument. Watching him, I felt a sudden surge of affection. I hadn't seen him so animated since he used to entertain my school friends with stories about volcanoes, and I suspect retirement frightened him more than he ever let on. Anyway, please come and visit soon. Mum is making her delicious lemon cake, and Dad has promised, not entirely convincingly, not to ask you about the meaning of life. Love, Ella

questions.prompt: Why does Ella think her father has thrown himself into philosophy?
options: He wants to prove that he is cleverer than his wife
Retiring worried him more than he was willing to show
He has always preferred philosophy to geography
He needs to pass an exam to complete his college course
questions.evidence: I suspect retirement frightened him more than he ever let on

options: Philosophy may not be discussed at Sunday lunch
Philosophical questions are not allowed early in the morning
Everyone must answer Dad's questions before eating
Dad must stop talking about free will at home
questions.evidence: declaring that philosophical questions are banned before ten in the morning

questions.prompt: What is the main purpose of Ella's email?
options: To describe a ferry crossing in detail
To ask Sam for help with a philosophy course
To tell Sam about their father's new passion and invite Sam to visit
To complain about their mother's rules
questions.evidence: Anyway, please come and visit soon.

questions.prompt: What does "animated" mean in "I hadn't seen him so animated"?
options: angry
confused
tired
lively and full of energy
questions.evidence: I hadn't seen him so animated

vocabulary.example: She gets really animated whenever someone mentions football.
Grandpa was carving the chicken while everyone waited.
The twins wore identical jackets to the party.
He spoke about his old teacher with real affection.
Attendance at the weekly meeting is expected.

expressions.note: 写信、发消息开头常用，带一点歉意：I've been meaning to call you.

expressions.meaning: 发生了有点离奇的转变
expressions.note: take a ... turn 表示事情朝某方向发展：take a turn for the worse“恶化”。
take up + 爱好，表示开始一项新活动，退休、换环境时常说：take up yoga.
带点夸张和幽默，形容某人变化很大，女性用 a changed woman。
多用于否定或比较：more than he let on“比他表现出来的更……”。
委婉的英式幽默，暗示对方的承诺不太靠得住。

knowledge.quote: I hadn't seen him so animated since he used to entertain my school friends with stories about volcanoes
knowledge.explanation: 过去完成时 hadn't seen + since，以渡轮上那一刻为参照点，说明在那之前很久没见过他这么兴奋，突出变化之大。

knowledge.quote: he asked whether goodness was something you were born with or something you practised
knowledge.explanation: whether ... or ... 引导宾语从句；转述问题时用陈述语序（goodness was），不用疑问语序，时态随 asked 变为过去时。

knowledge.quote: responded by sending the whole family a memo
knowledge.explanation: by + 动名词表示方式，“通过……来回应”；回答 How did she respond? 这类问题时很好用。

speaking: 用 1 分钟讲讲你家里某个人最近迷上的新爱好，以及它给家里带来的变化，用上 take up 和 a changed man/woman。
writing: 给一位老朋友写一封 180–220 词的邮件，分享一件让你哭笑不得的家庭趣事，开头用 I've been meaning to ...，结尾邀请对方来玩。

task.prompt: 仿照这句，用 ... the way other people ... 写一句话，用夸张的对比描述某人的习惯。
task.model: He now quotes ancient philosophers over breakfast the way other people read out the weather forecast.
